title: Cop31 live: EU and others reject deal as longest climate summit ever faces collapse
text:
Cop31 climate talks set to end in deep division as key deal rejected
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
Our colleagues in Antalya, Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn, have written about the outcome here.
'Australia left nothing on the field,' says Cop co-president Chris Bowen
Graham Readfearn
Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, has just spoken to reporters outside the plenary room. He says he hasn’t slept for three days.
“Unfortunately we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision and that’s very disappointing,” he said.
“Ultimately looking back many parties who are people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues and despite many many attempts on reflection those red lines were not able to be met.”
He thanked his staff for their efforts. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines they had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
He said one key red line was the language around the transition away from fossil fuels.
“Some parties insisted if it was mentioned, they would veto,” he said.
“Fossil fuels – we tried to strike a balance,” he said. “In the end it wasn’t enough... I would have been happy with transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support from parties. Given it’s the existing position of [previous] Cops... parties couldn’t live with that.”
He said “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and was irreversible, and happening at speed.
The electrification target, which was in the unadopted Antalya Pact, had a lot of support, he said, and it was not a deal breaker.
The UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres – right at the end of his term of office, has sent out a statement on the conference:
“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands.”
He doesn’t comment on the decision by countries to reject the text, but does say: “At COP28 in Dubai, all countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly and equitable manner. The task now is to accelerate that transition, finance and deliver it.
“I welcome countries coming forward with concrete plans to do so.’
Guterres has many times singled out fossil fuels for their role in the climate crisis.
Mohamed Adow, director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, says,
“This has been the worst ever COP and its collapse needs to be a wake up call for the world.
Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook.
COP31 was a ghost COP, and its lack of progress will haunt the climate vulnerable.
Despite progress in recent years agreeing to transition away from fossil fuels in 2023 and a promise to triple adaptation finance in 2025, this year everything ground to a halt. At a time when climate breakdown is only getting worse, this is unforgiveable.
Previous COP achievements show that the multilateral process is not to blame, it is the countries blocking progress on finance to accelerate climate action which that are ultimately responsible.”
Jasper Inventor, head of COP31 Greenpeace Delegation, says:
“We came to COP31 to end fossil fuels, not promote them and extend their lifeline. It’s bitterly disappointing to leave without a clear outcome or a credible pathway to end fossil fuels. We stopped a bad deal that favours fossil fuels, but leaving without a deal is still a failure for communities on the climate frontlines. As always, it is the world’s most vulnerable communities who bear the consequences of this failure. We’ve run out of time to avoid overshoot, but we can still keep 1.5°C alive.”
Tuvalu’s climate minister, Maina Talia, is now speaking. “There is significant work ahead of us”, he says, adding that we must transition away from fossil fuels in a way that is just. “Tuvalu cannot do this alone.”
China experts were critical of the approach taken by the presidency, and suggested that China could have been allowed to play a larger role.
Li Shuo, Director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said: “COP31 should have advanced global climate cooperation despite an increasingly difficult geopolitical landscape. Instead, Antalya represents a major setback for multilateral climate diplomacy — the most significant failure since Copenhagen.
“China may have seemed a quiet player at COP31, but its presence is increasingly self-assured and influential. As the global climate agenda faces mounting geopolitical and economic headwinds, Beijing is providing continuity and stability within the multilateral system. Unfortunately, the COP31 Presidency did not effectively deploy China’s discreet power in the chaotic final stages of the negotiations.”
Kate Logan, Director of China Climate Hub and Climate Diplomacy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said: “COP31 suffered in the hands of a disorganized presidency and stark geopolitical divides. With the US still sitting out and the EU facing down populism, China emphasized managing expectations and upholding multilateralism. While Beijing’s unique positioning enables it to forge alignment where few others can, China remained hesitant to step into a higher-profile role as consensus started to crumble.
“As the world’s dominant producer of clean technologies, China’s economic interests are increasingly intertwined with the objectives of climate talks. Officials highlighted how Chinese clean technologies are reducing emissions globally but trade protections raise costs and slow implementation, reflecting Beijing’s persistent frustration with tariffs that inhibit the free flow of clean tech. China’s $15 billion renewable energy deal with host Türkiye on the sidelines of COP31 shows how Beijing is advancing progress in the real economy, even if not necessarily captured by formal negotiations.”
Reaction to the breakdown of the talks, and the rejection of the key text, are flowing in from NGOs and campaigners.
Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth, said:
“After decades of broken pledges and hollow commitments, an agreement built on yet more empty promises would have been unforgivable and no substitute for the transformative action we urgently need. So the dramatic rejection of the Presidency’s final text by some, though underscoring the lack of consensus that’s been reached, restores some level of faith in its recognition that a deal of this calibre is no deal at all.”
He added:
“What matters now is not when governments reconvene, it’s how they do so. The world doesn’t need more meetings with wooly commitments. We need global governments, including the UK, to come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver. That means cutting emissions fairly at home, transitioning our economies in a way that leaves no one behind, and providing the public climate finance so desperately needed to protect people, livelihoods and our planet from unimaginable harm.”
Ani Dasguputa, president and CEO of the World Resources Institute, said:
“The hollow outcome at COP31 was a failure of political leadership, not a failure of the Paris Agreement. When narrow national interests override collective responsibility to confront the climate crisis, the entire world pays the price. Climate summits are not stages for posturing; they require every country to roll up their sleeves and do the hard work of finding ambitious common ground.
At a time when the science could not be clearer, it is indefensible that countries could not agree on even mentioning fossil fuels, the primary driver of climate change. The science has long settled this question – it’s time for the politics to catch up.”
Countries are still taking it in turns to speak in the plenary room. Despite a lack of consensus over the cover decision, Canada and others such as Fiji have said they want to continue discussions about oceans and strengthening the Cop process itself.
Canada concluded its statement saying “multilateralism is essential”.
Cop31 climate talks set to end in deep division as key deal rejected
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
Our colleagues in Antalya, Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn, have written about the outcome here.
Although parties are still speaking in the plenary hall, discussion is now swirling around the final outcome of the talks. The presidency has headed out to the hall to speak to the press, and has confirmed that there will be no new draft cover decision. There is a lot of confusion about the next steps here.
The talks have now all but collapsed. A number of side deals will be passed, but the number of rejections of the core deal continue to mount.
The Philippines are reminding the summit that without adequate resources they can’t deliver and express their profound concern over the lack of ambition around climate finance. “Developed countries responsibilities are not new.”
“People have every right to ask of us what have we been doing?”
Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign and Founding Director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation says:
“Parties were right to reject this text. It failed the people it was meant to protect. Rich countries refused to put money on the table to help communities prepare for and recover from climate disasters, and handed polluters a free pass instead. No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure. But this cannot become an excuse for more delay: the money and the plan must now come.
“This text would have made Antalya the COP that opened the floodgates to carbon capture. It deleted the renewables target, handed the fossil fuel industry a gigatonne-scale lifeline, and would have licensed land grabs from Indigenous Peoples and farmers in the Global South. Its rejection must close those floodgates for good.”
Now we hear from the Fiji climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, and she says the country is deeply disappointed that consensus has not been reached.
And then she speaks to the Australian minister, Chris Bowen, directly.
“You have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it. Your door has always been open. This work is hard - sleepless nights, and over hours and days of constant negotiations. This is not easy but we do it and we do it for our people.
“The failure here is not yours to carry. It is the responsibility of all parties.”
She said that the 1.5C Paris global heating target was the “limit of our survival” and access to finance was the means to survival.
She was followed by Belize, who said it rejected the Antalya Pact text.
And Peru which says the Cop process needs significant reforms.
President acknowledges no agreement on the draft text
A short while ago Cop president Murat Kurum acknowledged that there was no agreement on the draft text and the decisions had not been adopted. However the talks are continuing, and there is still no formal decision.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a “take it or leave it” demand. It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”
The countries that have objected so far include the EU, Marshall Islands, Norway, Panama and Vanuatu. Many others have expressed dissatisfaction.
The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has issued a statement:
“This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it.
“The moment required bold ambition, and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.
“This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis.
“Our commitment to multilateralism and protecting our communities from the realities of overshoot is unwavering.”
The UK says they could not find consensus on the deal
The UK has now spoken, saying they have been working to find compromise: “this is why we could not find consensus on this deal”.
“It moves us backwards, it is the lowest common denominator when it should have been uniting us in action.”
She says the critical areas to work on going forward are climate finance, and says they have been disappointed not to provide the clarity that partners need. The other areas are reducing emissions in line with 1.5, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and reducing methane and non CO2 emissions.
India is speaking now on behalf of the Like-Minded Developing Countries. The delegate says that they want to keep working. So not an acceptance but also not an outright rejection.
Responding to the EU’s rejection of the COP31 cover text, Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, said:
“The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create. Adaptation, finance and the Just Transition mechanism are dead in the water, while loss and damage has been systematically erased from these talks. For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition. Without money and credible action at home, those demands are hollow. The EU cannot help sabotage the negotiations, then pose as the climate conscience of the world.”
